annotatedSteps.description: Proof of identity in general terms using standard trigonometric identities
annotatedSteps.studentWork:
Put A = 30°. cos 30° = √3/2 , cosec 30° = 2
LHS = (1 - 3/4) × 4 = 1/4 × 4 = 1 = RHS
Hence proved.
annotatedSteps.teacherAnnotation: × A numerical verification for a specific angle does not constitute a mathematical proof of an identity.
annotatedSteps.correctedWorking:
LHS = (1 - cos²A) · cosec²A
Using identity 1 - cos²A = sin²A:
= sin²A · cosec²A
= sin²A · (1 / sin²A)
= 1 = RHS
Hence proved.

teacherNote: Marked against: Writing LHS and using trigonometric identity 1 - cos²A = sin²A (1.5); Substituting cosec A = 1/sin A (or cosec²A = 1/sin²A) to simplify LHS (1); Simplifying to 1 and concluding LHS = RHS (0.5). To prove a trigonometric identity, you must use standard identities valid for all general angles A rather than substituting a specific numerical value like 30°. Start with LHS = (1 - cos²A)cosec²A = sin²A · (1/sin²A) = 1 = RHS. This method does not work in general, so the working built on it cannot earn method marks — use a method that holds in every case.
